A DP student picking three Higher Level (HL) subjects is picking three HL internal assessments, each with a school-set draft deadline, and those deadlines do not politely space themselves out. The group you choose in also matters: a science taken at HL brings a written investigation with data analysis and uncertainty treatment, while a Group 3 individuals and societies subject brings an essay-shaped task that rewards sourcing and argument instead.

Subject choice across both boards, HL and SL decisions, and the internal assessments each one carries are the conversation we have most often with Wadala parents in the term before options are locked. The question to ask is not which subject is easier. It is which subject your child can still work at in March of the second year, when three IAs, the Extended Essay (EE) and the Theory of Knowledge (TOK) essay are all live at once. A subject a student quietly dislikes becomes the one that is dropped from the revision timetable first.

Where a tutor adds real value on subject depth is in the mechanics of a task rather than its content. Knowing the chemistry is one thing; knowing that an investigation needs a research question narrow enough to be answered with the apparatus a Mumbai school lab actually has is another. For structure, weighting and current requirements, read the live subject guide or ask your school's IB coordinator rather than trusting any figure quoted online, including ours, because the IB revises guides on its own cycle.

Middle Years Programme reports score each subject against criteria A to D on seven-point bands, so a student can look strong on knowledge and still be losing most of the available marks on analysis or on communication. A tutor should read the report with you, name the criterion that is actually costing marks, and then work on that specific skill rather than on the subject in general. Parents who do this in Year 3 of MYP tend to have a much easier Diploma Programme conversation two years later.

faqs.question: What happens if there is no progress after a month?
faqs.answer: Tell us at four weeks rather than waiting for the next report. The first thing we look at is the diagnosis, not the tutor, because the most common cause of a stalled month is a wrong starting point: the sessions have been teaching Year 11 content to a student whose gap is two years earlier. That is fixable without changing anyone. If the fit is genuinely wrong, we arrange a replacement using the brief you already gave us, so you are not starting the search from the beginning. Either way, a month of nothing is information and should be acted on quickly.

faqs.question: What if the tutor is competent but my child simply does not get on with them?
faqs.answer: That is a legitimate reason to change and you do not need to justify it beyond saying so. Subject knowledge is necessary and not sufficient; a student who dreads the session will stop doing the homework between sessions, which is where most of the gain actually comes from. Tell us what did not work, in whatever words you have, because specifics help the next match. We keep the programme, level and slot from your original request and look again. Most second matches hold, because the first attempt has usually taught everyone something useful about what this particular student needs.

faqs.question: Which months are the real pressure points for IB families in Mumbai?
faqs.answer: September and October, then February and March. The year opens quietly in June, which is exactly when foundation work is cheapest to do and most often skipped. The first serious assessments arrive by October, along with Extended Essay supervisor meetings for DP1. The hardest stretch is February into March, when internal assessment final submissions, mock examinations and the Theory of Knowledge essay land inside a few weeks of each other for a DP2 student. Families who arrange support in June are buying teaching; families who arrange it in January are buying triage, which costs more effort for less movement.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover more than one IB subject for the same student?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth being sceptical about when. Maths and Physics at Standard Level, or two sciences in MYP, are a reasonable pairing for one person. Three Higher Level subjects across different groups is not, however confident the tutor sounds. The test is whether they can describe the assessed task for each subject in specific terms rather than general ones. We would rather send you two specialists for two subjects than one person stretched across both, and we will say so even when it means a more complicated schedule for your household.

faqs.question: Do you work with students from JBCN International School, Parel or Don Bosco International School?
faqs.answer: We work with students who attend them, which is a different thing from working with the schools. IB Gram is an independent platform and is not affiliated with either school or with any school named anywhere on this site, and no tutor we introduce represents a school's own programme. What the school does determine is the calendar: internal deadlines, mock timing and reporting cycles come from them, so a tutor should be planning around your school's dates rather than a generic schedule. Send us the term calendar if you have it and the planning gets noticeably sharper.

faqs.question: Where in the home should lessons actually happen?
faqs.answer: At a table in a shared room, with the door open. Bedrooms invite distraction and make it harder for a parent to hear whether teaching is happening or whether the hour has become supervised homework. A dining table with the television off, decent light and both the textbook and the marked work to hand is genuinely better than a dedicated study with a closed door. For families in compact Wadala flats, clearing one table for a fixed two hours a week is usually the whole solution. Keep a notebook for the session in that spot so nothing is hunted for at the start.
